syllabus.clause: with HDR histograms, and avoid coordinated omission in load generators.
Criterion and Divan for wall-clock benchmarks; instruction-count benchmarks (iai-callgrind, renamed Gungraun) for stable CI signals.

items.item: warmup runs the routine repeatedly first, giving the OS, CPU, and JIT time to adapt, which prevents cold caches and compilation time from throwing off the later measurements
outlier classification uses a modified version of Tukey's Method, computing the interquartile range from the difference between the 25th and 75th percentile
the comparison process can be extremely sensitive to small, unrelated changes such as differences in background load, which can make it falsely detect an optimization or a regression

at.step: Criterion.rs's own documentation and HdrHistogram's own README both describe this exact discipline directly: real warmup and outlier classification before trusting a result, and a real correction for exactly the missed, slow samples a naive measurement would hide. Does this topic's own code measure the identical real divergence those real tools exist to catch?

items.item: a raw histogram collected under coordinated omission can show the overwhelming majority of results as fast, which is obviously not right, once a long pause is hidden behind a single sample

recording with an expected interval between samples produces a data set that much more accurately reflects the response-time distribution a random, uncoordinated request would actually have experienced

The percentile function uses the nearest-rank method (sort, then index directly by rank) rather than interpolating between two samples, so every reported percentile is one of the real recorded samples, never a synthetic value between two of them.

at.step: Measured: the real p50 and the real p99 of the identical distribution are genuinely separate statistics, computed from the identical real samples

items.item: The 'before' and 'after' distributions are both fixed, hardcoded arrays rather than generated by any random process, because this sandboxed container has no flaky wall-clock timing to depend on and the chapter plan requires a real, deterministic cost model standing in for a real benchmark's own captured samples.

at.step: A benchmark's own average goes down after a change. Does that genuinely mean every real user's own request got faster?

items.item: The p50-improved-and-p99-regressed claim is checked as a conjunction of two separate comparisons on the same two arrays, not as a single derived number, so the test would fail if either half of the claimed divergence did not actually hold.

at.step: Measured: the real median genuinely improved, while the real p99 genuinely regressed, on the identical change

items.item: The average-hides-the-regression claim is checked by requiring the average to have genuinely improved at the same time the p99 genuinely regressed, not merely by computing the average; a sample design where the average also got worse would fail this check rather than silently passing.

at.step: Measured: the real average genuinely improved too, completely hiding the real p99's own regression

items.item: The sample arrays are deliberately designed so the outlier's own worsening (a small delta spread over one of twenty samples) is outweighed by the bulk improvement (a larger delta spread over the other nineteen), which is what makes the average's own improvement genuine rather than an artifact of a differently shaped distribution.

at.step: Measured: the real average genuinely improved too, completely hiding the real p99's own regression
